p: If you know a Dimitris, you probably know October 26. Χρόνια πολλά. Many years. Maybe it's a phone call from your mother. A visit from a friend. A box of sweets brought to the door. In many Greek families, a name day is more than a date on the calendar. You might have celebrated it your whole life. You know the greeting. You know the church. You may even know the icon. How much do you know about the person behind the name?

I went to Greek school. I never learned any of this. Why is Saint Demetrios sometimes shown on a horse, striking a fallen ruler? Why did shepherds once use his feast day to mark the turning of the seasons? And how did one saint become so tied to a city that its liberation is remembered on his feast day? Even historians still debate how much we can know about the real Demetrios. What is certain is how early, and how strongly, one city made him its own.

According to Orthodox tradition, Demetrios was a young officer in Thessaloniki. He was imprisoned for his Christian faith, killed by spears in the early fourth century. The Church also remembers Nestor, a young follower who, according to the story, defeated a formidable gladiator and was himself put to death. But historians ask a different question. What can the surviving evidence actually establish? So we hold two things side by side. What the Church remembers. And what the historical record allows us to know.

By the seventh century, written collections of miracles described Saint Demetrios protecting Thessaloniki during attacks. In those stories, he appears on the city walls. A rider on a white horse. A figure in a white cloak, moving along the ramparts at night. For believers, he became the city's protector. A great basilica had risen at a place associated by tradition with his martyrdom. At its heart stood a six-sided silver shrine, where the faithful came to pray.
After a fire in the seventh century, it was restored. In 1493, under Ottoman rule, it became a mosque. Even then, veneration of the saint continued in one corner of the building.

And then, centuries later, October 26 took on another meaning. In the autumn of 1912, during the First Balkan War, Greek forces approached Thessaloniki. But they weren't the only army approaching the city. Bulgarian forces were moving toward it too. The Ottoman commander agreed to surrender Thessaloniki to the Greeks. Papers were signed after midnight. But the date written on them was October 26, by the calendar Greece used then. The feast of Saint Demetrios.

Why that date? Accounts differ. Some say it was for the saint. Others point to the Bulgarian army, hours away. Within days, King George the First entered the city. The basilica, which had served as a mosque for centuries, returned to Christian worship. To this day, Thessaloniki remembers both its patron saint and its liberation on October 26.

In August 1917, a devastating fire swept through Thessaloniki. The Basilica of Saint Demetrios was left almost in ruins. But not everything was lost. Parts of the ancient structure survived, along with the remarkable early mosaics. The building was painstakingly restored and returned to worship in the late 1940s. Beneath it lies a crypt incorporating part of an ancient Roman bath, associated by tradition with the saint's imprisonment and death. Since 1988, the basilica had been included among Thessaloniki's UNESCO-listed early Christian and Byzantine monuments.

In early images, Saint Demetrios doesn't look like the mounted warrior many people recognize today. He appears as a young man in a court dress. Later, around the tenth century, images increasingly show him with a spear and shield. The martyr had become a warrior saint. And later still, we find another image. Demetrios riding a horse. Someone lies beneath his spear. Who is that man? To understand, we have to travel to the year 1207.

A Bulgarian ruler named Kaloyan was besieging Thessaloniki. But he never took the city. He died during the campaign. Soon people were saying that Saint Demetrios himself had struck Kaloyan with a spear. Medieval writers recorded it within a decade. Historians still debate how Kaloyan actually died. One chronicler blamed illness. Many historians suspect one of his own commanders. On some later icons, the fallen figure beneath Demetrios's spear represents Kaloyan. Not the gladiator from the story of Nestor.

A ruler from a conflict that happened centuries after the saint's traditional lifetime. An icon isn't a photograph of the past. But it can reveal how a community remembered its history, its fears, and its faith.

read.h: Myrrh, pilgrims and a great fair
p: The Orthodox Church gives Saint Demetrios another title. Μυροβλύτης. The Myrrh-Streamer. According to Orthodox tradition, fragrant myrrh flowed from his shrine. Over the centuries, stories of healing and protection became part of his veneration. Pilgrims traveled to Thessaloniki and carried home small flasks associated with the saint's myrrh. They turned up far beyond the city. And his feast wasn't only a religious occasion. In the twelfth century, a satirical Byzantine work called the Timarion described a great fair held around the celebration.

Merchants came from distant regions. Cloth, imported goods, horses, cattle. Centuries later, relics venerated as those of Saint Demetrios returned to Thessaloniki from Italy. His head was returned in October 1978, followed by other relics in April 1980.

In Thessaloniki, the celebrations begin the day before, with services and a procession of his relics. And on the feast itself, Thessaloniki also remembers its liberation in 1912. Since 1966, the Dimitria culture festival has carried his name into another part of the city's life. But outside the city, Saint Demetrios's day once meant something else. For shepherds, the year had two important turning points. On Saint George's day in spring, the flocks went up toward the mountain pastures.

On Saint Demetrios's day in autumn, they came back down. An old saying recorded in the Peloponnese puts it simply. Saint George opens them. Saint Demetrios closes them. And there's another tradition I didn't know. In Thrace, people had a saying for the unexpected warm weather that could arrive around his feast. Saint Demetrios brings a little summer. Today, in Greece and in the Greek Orthodox communities around the world, October 26 remains his feast day.

Churches following the old Julian calendar observe it on November 8 according to the civil calendar. In some American parishes dedicated to Saint Demetrios, celebrations begin the evening before with Vespers and the blessing of five loaves. And at home, for people named Dimitris, Dimitrios, or Dimitra, the celebration can connect them to someone who came before them. Maybe a grandfather. Maybe a grandmother. Maybe someone whose name a family wanted to carry into another generation.

read.h: The questions we can still ask
p: Sometimes we keep a tradition simply because it was always part of home. We love it before we fully understand it. Then years passed. And the people who could have explained it aren't always there when we're finally ready to ask. But the questions don't have to end there. We can still search. In history. And sacred art. The words of the Church. In archives, and in the memories of people who still carry those traditions.

So next time someone asks why we celebrate a name day, we can give them more than "That's just what we've always done." And if your name is Dimitris, Dimitrios, or Dimitra, here's something worth asking. Who were you named after? What do you know about their story? If someone in your family still remembers, ask them. Χρόνια πολλά to all those who celebrate Ai-Dimitri and named after the saint.
